Inception

in-SEP-shun — contains 'cept,' to take hold; at its inception, an idea first takes hold. · noun

What It Means

Inception is the starting point at which something begins.

The club has kept a photo from every single meeting since its inception fifteen years ago.

Worked Example

A tiny lemonade stand run by two kids on a single summer weekend eventually grows into a chain of shops across the state. Years later, a reporter asks the founders to describe exactly how it all first started.

The very first moment something began — before any of the later growth — is its inception. Unlike 'history,' which covers the whole span of time, inception points specifically to the beginning.

Antonyms

termination: the act of ending something

How Strong Is It? — start → inception → genesis

start vs. inception

start vs. inception: Start is a plainer, weaker word than inception — start can refer to any beginning, casual or formal, while inception specifically marks the formal beginning of something significant.

genesis vs. inception

genesis vs. inception: Genesis can feel even more significant than inception: both mark a beginning, but genesis often implies the very origin of something enormous or foundational.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: into, on (Latin)

Root — cept

Root — cept: to take, to seize (from Latin capere; its past form -cept- appears in accept and intercept)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or process of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In- (into) + cept (to take, to seize — from Latin capere) + -ion (act or process of): Latin incipere meant 'to begin,' literally 'to take hold of.' The inception of something is the moment it is first taken hold of and set into motion.

Use the root in a new word: capture

Use the root in a new word: capture: The photographer waited patiently to capture the exact moment the eagle took flight.
